# Trajectory Learning Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts II through IV built closure around a fixed model. @Sec-vol3-evaluation ended Part IV by measuring task acceptance and comparing configurations, then testing explanations for failures under declared conditions. Part V changes the model itself. Training changes the proposals the runtime receives; it does not grant authority or remove the runtime's enforcement obligations. A changed policy can still alter the realized trajectory length, state use, and requested effects, so its behavior needs evaluation under those same contracts. Diagnostic findings help compare a training intervention with changes to context, tools, or the runtime, without requiring every failure to have one exclusive cause. Curation decides which recorded trajectories support a particular learning use. Held-out evaluation and release policies then govern whether the resulting model may replace the one in service.

::: {#pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training .callout-principle title="Verified trajectory post-training"}

**Invariant**: A recorded outcome does not determine how a trajectory should be used for learning. Curation relates the evidence to a proposed behavior change, distinguishes admissible targets from contextual or rejected actions, and preserves the conditions under which the record was assessed. Recovery demonstrations expose decisions after errors that an error-free corpus does not cover; their value still depends on the intended tasks and learning objective. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-flywheel-gap and @sec-vol3-flywheel-curation.

**Implication**: A curation pipeline compares training with other system interventions, declares the consumer of each admitted record, and selects coverage and targets under a versioned data contract. Passing a task check does not automatically make every action in its trace a suitable demonstration.

:::

Once a trajectory is admitted, the imitation objective must distinguish the responses selected for learning from the context that supports them.

::: {#pri-vol3-action-masked-loss .callout-principle title="Observation loss masking"}

**Invariant**: For policy-response imitation, delivered observations condition the selected responses but are not themselves response targets. Predicting observation tokens adds a different objective; it does not turn generated text into authentic tool evidence. Context tokens can still affect gradients through the predictions that depend on them. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking.

**Implication**: Construct the loss mask from the admitted target spans and the actual serialized input, not from authorship alone. Preserve necessary conditioning information, specify how turn endings and incomplete responses are treated, and evaluate the resulting policy under the intended serving format. Masking changes supervision; the runtime still controls tool execution and evidence delivery.

:::

Imitation learns from selected responses, while preference learning compares assessed alternatives. Reinforcement learning instead collects new interactions and uses their rewards to guide policy updates.

::: {#pri-vol3-verifiable-rewards .callout-principle title="Reinforcement learning against isolated verifiers"}

**Invariant**: Reinforcement learning turns the reward check into the objective. The policy learns whatever the check rewards, including any route by which it can reach and change the check, and it learns nothing the check does not test. The gradient also vanishes unless the policy already succeeds on some attempts and fails on others. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-rlvr-need and @sec-vol3-rlvr-sandboxing.

**Implication**: An RL pipeline runs the verifier in an isolated environment that receives only the policy's output artifact, judges the trained policy on held-out tests the reward never saw, and starts from a supervised policy whose pass rate is above zero.

:::

The three chapters form one pipeline, each consuming what the one before it produced. @Sec-vol3-trajectory-curation triages failures, rebuilds their tasks as resettable fixtures, and admits trajectories through a cascade of checks the agent cannot reach, sorting them into a supervised mix of clean and recovery trajectories and a separate pool of hard negatives. @Sec-vol3-fine-tuning trains on the supervised mix by imitation, with the loss aimed at the policy's own tokens. @Sec-vol3-rlvr starts from that fine-tuned policy, whose nonzero pass rate it needs, and optimizes against isolated verifiers where no demonstration reaches. All three depend on the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}), which makes running a stated check on every trajectory affordable and leaves the soundness of that check as the limit on what training can learn. Weights change how likely a proposal is to pass, never the authority to act on it. Part VI takes the resulting agent from one trajectory to many.
